entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @javadimr

TV has always been political, favoring the hard core. But what television lacks today is attention to the interests of the cultural middle class. Previously, ordinary people — despite their dissatisfaction with TV's political slant — were viewers of compelling films and series, children's programming, sports, and documentaries. Programs with 80% viewership were not the exception.

entry.title: [javadimr] Two influential social blocs today are the "cultural middle class" and the…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @javadimr

Two influential social blocs today are the "cultural middle class" and the "hard core." The former, after 18 Dey, faced a crisis of trust, doubt about the effectiveness of collective action, and a kind of erosion of political hope; the latter, after 9 Esfand, grew in internal cohesion, self-confidence, and capacity for mobilization. Iran's future (quite apart from the question of the war's outcome and the question of the economy) depends to a large extent on how the relationship between these two blocs evolves: whether the possibility of coexistence and temporary coalitions between them takes shape, or whether tension and polarization intensify; and also on the extent to which the government can mediate among the demands, sensitivities, and sources of power of both and create a balance. Note: I did not intend to reduce the entire cultural middle class to the protesters and rioters of 18 Dey. The distinction between the 18-Dey-ers and the 401-ers is also important. But the issue is the condition of the cultural middle class after 18 Dey — they were both depressed and angry, whether or not they had taken part in the protests.

Source: @javadimr

The definition of being unveiled has changed in society, and women who don't cover their heads are no longer considered unveiled. To most women, "being unveiled" is synonymous with showing off one's body. With norms having shifted and society transformed, one can no longer speak and act the way we used to. By "the past," I mean the year 1403, not several decades ago!

"On the condition that beforehand..." One can use the subsidiary plan of a car-free day, provided that car imports have been liberalized beforehand. One can make dress code rules mandatory in official places, provided that we first accept the public's customary view on dress in public places. The rule of governance is deference to the opinion of the majority of the people.

entry.title: [javadimr] The person who posted this film tweeted: "Sir, it's impossible—we must uproot…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @javadimr

The person who posted this film tweeted: "Sir, it's impossible—we must uproot everything and build from scratch..." But I don't hold such a view. In my opinion, there's no need to uproot everything. In the absence of a government that is willing and able to deal with violators—and deal with them equally—our driving situation is acceptable; because the current order in driving, especially in Tehran, is the product of people interacting with each other in the absence of the government (in the sense of the state) and the police. We are left to our own devices, but we haven't gone out of control. People are good; the blame lies elsewhere. And of course, driving is a symbol and a sign of how the country is administered.
